n1.method: Every line and transformer of 100 kV and up is taken out once: with the headline's 3 campuses and their upgrades connected, with all 8 of the search and theirs, and with no campus (the model's own baseline). Flows after each outage come from line outage distribution factors on the network's own factorization (DC power flow; the plants keep their output); a line or transformer is a problem past 115 % of its rating (an assumed emergency rating: the dataset gives one rating). Outages that cut off load are skipped, as the model would strand it on its own. One that cuts off only a plant moves its output to the other plants when they have the room; when they don't, it is a problem of its own (short of generation: the state would have to stop exporting or cut customers). The counts are outages, not overloads: one outage can push several lines past their rating.
n1.sentence: Single-outage screen (N-1) of 2,822 outages, with the headline's 3 campuses and their upgrades: 78 single outages push a line or transformer past 115 % of its rating where the model alone doesn't, or push it further (the model alone has 94 outages that push something past 115 %). With all 8 campuses of the search: 118 single outages push a line or transformer past 115 % of its rating where the model alone doesn't, or push it further; in 4 more, the other plants can't make up the output of a plant the outage cuts off (4 of them would cut customers, up to 954 MW).

capacity.method: Campuses go in one at a time, each where it fits with every campus so far (an exact power-flow solve). When none fits, the 30 sites closest to fitting are each solved with the campus there, the lines it would push past their rating are raised to a standard level and priced, and the cheapest bundle is built. With every line in service (N-0), the final set runs through the cascade engine: nothing trips. That checks N-0 only; a single-outage (N-1) screen of the headline's campuses follows.
